perpetual-traveller-schultz-hill.story:
A perpetual traveller, sometimes shortened to PT, is a person who bases different parts of their life in different countries and avoids staying long enough in any of them to count as a legal resident. The stated aim is to reduce taxes and civic duties such as jury duty and military service, and to gain personal freedom.
The framing idea is flag theory. It is credited to the investment writer Harry D. Schultz, who proposed that everyone should have a second passport and an address in a tax haven, and that assets should be kept outside the home country. It was later expanded to five flags, adding a place where money is earned and a place for recreation.
The idea was spread by Scope International Limited, a company in Waterlooville, England. It published books in the 1980s and 1990s under the name W.G. Hill, which may have been a pseudonym, and sold them through classified advertisements in The Times. One of them, published around 1989, was said to have been inspired and edited by Schultz, and a later handbook followed in 1993. Companies marketing offshore centres and tax schemes have used the idea as a staple.
It was never a place and it claimed no territory, so no state ever had to shut it down. Who actually wrote the books is not firmly documented.

icrc-headquarters-agreement.story:
The International Committee of the Red Cross is based in Geneva, and on 19 March 1993 it signed a headquarters agreement with the Swiss Federal Council at Berne, taking effect at once. It is an example of a body founded privately that gained a state's written recognition of its standing, so it is a useful marker for how far this kind of deal can go.
Under Article 1, Switzerland recognises its international juridical personality and its legal capacity. Under Article 3, no Swiss public official may enter its premises without its express consent. Under Article 5, it has immunity from legal process and from execution, except where its president formally waives it, in civil claims over its vehicles, in staff disputes, in counter-claims tied to its own proceedings and in enforcing an arbitration settlement made under the agreement. Article 6 exempts it from most direct and indirect taxes.
The host kept some things. Non-Swiss staff stay in part of the Swiss social insurance system under Article 12, and Article 13 leaves them liable for civil claims from vehicle use and for road traffic fines. Article 20 says Switzerland bears no international responsibility for what the organisation or its staff do. Article 21 gives the foreign ministry the job of carrying out the agreement.
The agreement protects an organisation in order to allow it to do its work. It gives the body no territory and no people. Its staff are ordinary residents and nationals of their own countries, within the limits listed.

icrc-swiss-agreement.story:
The International Committee of the Red Cross began in Geneva in 1863, after Henry Dunant's book on the wounded of war. In 1864 delegates from sixteen countries met, and representatives of twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention. Today it is the only institution explicitly named in international humanitarian law as a controlling authority, with a mandate from the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 and its own statutes.
It is a private Swiss association, and its governing committee limits membership to Swiss nationals, chosen by the committee itself. Contrary to a common belief, it is not a sovereign body like the Order of Malta. Yet it holds many of the protections of a state. A formal agreement with the Swiss government of 19 March 1993 protects all its property in Switzerland, including its headquarters and archive, grants members and staff legal immunity, exempts it from taxes and fees, guarantees protected and duty-free transfer of goods, services and money, and gives it secure communications at the same level as foreign embassies. Switzerland does not recognise passports it issues.
It holds similar privileges in other countries through agreements or national law, and in some cases through court decisions, such as the right of delegates not to testify before international tribunals. On 16 October 1990 the UN General Assembly gave it observer status, the first private organisation to receive it, and the UN lists it among entities with a standing invitation as an observer.
It shows how much protection of the kind a state enjoys can be given to a body that is not a state. The protection was granted for its work, it comes from agreements one government at a time, and it gives no authority over any land or people.

sky-cruise.story:
Sky Cruise is an idea for a giant nuclear-powered flying hotel, shown in an animated video that Hashem Al-Ghaili released in mid-2022. The original design came from an art director, Tony Holmsten, who drew it over a decade earlier. It exists only as images, and no base, company or site has been named, so it has no place on the ground.
The video shows a craft carrying up to 5,000 people and staying in the air for years, with passengers and supplies arriving on commercial and private jets that land on it. Coverage of the video described its power as nuclear fusion, and Al-Ghaili separately said he expected small nuclear reactors for aircraft to be available in the 2030s. Viewers questioned its aerodynamics and whether it could fly at all, and Al-Ghaili himself stressed that it is only a concept. The project is on the map as the best-known image of a home that never touches land.
Staying in the air would not take it outside national law. Under the Chicago Convention, the main treaty on civil flying, an aircraft has the nationality of the country that registers it, and every jet shuttling people to it would have to leave from a licensed airport in some country. Whether any regulator would certify such a craft is unknown, because none has been asked. No such aircraft has been built.

zaqistan.story:
Zaqistan is a four-acre patch of desert in northwestern Box Elder County, Utah, in the United States, which its owner calls a country. Zaq Landsberg, a New York resident, bought the land online in about 2005, when it was only numbers on a GPS to him, and he calls himself its president. The site is about 60 miles from the nearest town and 15 miles from a paved road, followed by a two-mile hike off a dirt track. He keeps the exact location private so that people do not get lost looking for it.
Over several visits he has set up a flag, a border gate, a supply bunker and a robot sentry. He also makes official-looking passports, which visitors can have stamped on the way in and out. He says the project works best when the passports circulate in the real world.
Landsberg calls it an art project that tests the limits of land ownership and sovereignty. He has said that his goal is for it to become a real country and that this is impossible, and that he is going through the motions to find out what those words mean. No country recognises it. He pays property tax to the county and calls these payments tributes, to keep relations friendly. He is not known to have any dispute with the county. The land stays in Utah under American law.

republic-of-montmartre.story:
The Republic of Montmartre is a charitable association of artists in the Montmartre district of Paris, France, run in the style of a mock republic. Montmartre is the hilltop neighbourhood long associated with painters and cabarets. The association was created in 1921, after the First World War, to protect the character of the district from property developers and to keep alive the artists' habit of helping one another. The City of Paris credits the illustrator Joe Bridge with proposing it on 7 May 1921, while a list of micronations names the cartoonist Jean Barrez.
It has a president, ministers, ambassadors and more than 500 volunteer members, who wear a red scarf, black cape and black hat. Its motto means doing good with joy. The republic's work is ordinary charity. It holds Christmas celebrations for disadvantaged children, gives money to groups that work with disadvantaged children, and runs exhibitions, book fairs and concerts. It remains active today.
It has no separate status in French law. The form of a state is used here for fun and fundraising, with no claim against France. Its offices and ministers are titles within an association.

set.founder: Joe Bridge and Montmartre artists, according to the City of Paris; a list of micronations names Jean Barrez

shanhaiwoo.story:
ShanhaiWoo, written 山海坞 in Chinese, is a series of pop-up cities, meaning temporary communities that gather in one place for a limited time and call themselves a city. People who work on cryptocurrency and related technology come together for weeks, live near one another and build projects. A list of such gatherings by the newsletter Agartha places it in China and Thailand, and a report by IOSG counts it among the communities that met in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in October 2024.
Its Singapore edition gives the clearest picture of how it runs. It was a one-month village from 2 September to 1 October 2025, open to up to 200 builders by application, covering Ethereum, artificial intelligence and related technology. Early teams valued under $30 million could apply. Participants chose their own hotels, with discounts offered, and the programme began with a town hall meeting on 4 September and an opening ceremony on 5 September. Backers named on the event page include DRK Lab, AltLayer, Blockchain Builders Fund and HashKey Capital, and a limited number of scholarships, each worth about $2,500, covered part of the airfare and 30 days in shared lodging.
No individual founders are named, and attendance at earlier editions is not known. Its participants are visitors, who remain under the law of the host country, and it makes no claim on territory. Writers on such gatherings describe them as a possible first step towards permanent communities.

zuzalu.story:
Zuzalu was a temporary community of about 200 people at Lustica Bay, a resort on the Adriatic coast of Montenegro. It was conceived by Vitalik Buterin, a co-founder of the Ethereum cryptocurrency network, and ran for about two months from 25 March 2023. It set the model for later pop-up cities, in which people who met online live in one place for weeks or months.
Participants came from crypto, drug companies, politics and universities. They stayed mostly in resort hotels and rented homes, with the five-star Chedi Lustica Bay as the main base. Topics included cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and the science of longer life, and the longevity group VitaDAO helped organise a three-day science conference. A main theme of that track was finding a new jurisdiction and set of rules for longevity medicine.
Another topic was the network state, an idea from the former Coinbase executive Balaji Srinivasan in which an online community eventually buys land and seeks its own laws. Srinivasan appeared remotely. The news site Decrypt reported that some compared the event to Burning Man for futurists and others to a sleepaway camp for the crypto elite.
Daily life was loosely organised. Talks and seminars were arranged by participants, breakfast was served every day at a local restaurant taken over for the event, and a philosophy group met in the hotel sauna until the sessions were shut down after more than 30 people began attending. One group handed out worthless Venezuelan bolivar notes as party invitations, then built an app that used the serial numbers as a test identity system. The writer Jonathan Hillis later called the location too expensive and inconvenient, and said it had produced no longer-term plan for a permanent base.
No land was taken and no new law was reported. Everyone remained under Montenegrin law and went home when the two months were over. Later projects, including Vitalia and Zuitzerland, grew out of it. It tested how a community organises itself and asked nothing of the host country's law.

artemis-project-europa.story:
In 1997 the private Artemis Project drafted a plan to settle Europa, a moon of Jupiter whose surface is ice over a hidden ocean. It proposed igloos on the surface as bases for drilling through the ice to explore the water below, and it suggested people could live in air pockets inside the ice. That ocean may hold more than twice the water of all Earth's oceans, though metals and minerals would have to be brought in.
Radiation is the main barrier, because Jupiter's radiation belts cover Europa. An unshielded person would take about 5.40 sieverts a day, sieverts being a measure of radiation dose, which would be fatal within a short time. Heavy shielding might make a research base possible. The plan was never carried out.
The law asks something of even a private plan like this. Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty makes each state answer for its citizens' activities in space and requires authorisation and supervision, so the project would have needed a government's approval before leaving Earth. No such approval is recorded. Article II would have stopped any such government from claiming Europa on the settlers' behalf, and Article IX tells states to avoid harmful contamination of other worlds, a concern for an ocean that might hold life.

grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.story:
Grand Capri Republic and Atlantis, Isle of Gold were two rival plans to found new countries on Triumph and Long Reefs, two coral reefs about four and a half miles off southeast Florida near Miami. The reefs are underwater except for brief exposure at low tide. In the early 1960s the United States claimed only a narrow belt of sea as its own, and these reefs lay beyond it, so the promoters believed no state could stop them building. A court later called them reefs underlying the high seas.
Louis M. Ray and his firm, Acme General Contractors, planned Grand Capri, a resort island. They placed caissons, large watertight boxes, on the reefs and filled them with material dredged from the seabed. A rival, Atlantis Development Corporation, said an earlier discovery gave it better title and planned commercial buildings on pilings. So two private parties were arguing over who owned reefs that lay under water at high tide.
The first official contact was a building permit. On 16 November 1964 Acme applied to the US Army Corps of Engineers, the federal agency that regulates building in waterways, to build a 20-acre resort island. The application itself suggested that Acme expected US rules to matter. The Corps refused, and Ray dredged anyway.
The government went to court. A trial court in southern Florida ordered a temporary halt in April 1965. In January 1969 it barred construction but rejected the government's trespass claim, because the government did not own the reefs. That raised the key question. Trespass means entering someone else's property, and the United States did not own the reefs, so it needed some other legal ground for stopping a builder.
The government appealed. In 1970 the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit answered that question in United States v. Ray. It held that the reefs were part of the outer continental shelf, the seabed extending from the coast. US law and the 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf give the United States exclusive rights there to explore and exploit resources. It also held the work unlawful for a second reason. The builders had no permit from the Secretary of the Army, and a federal law on the continental shelf, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, extends that permit rule to fixed structures on the shelf. The court said that neither ownership nor possession is needed for such an order, and it ordered full and permanent relief against any interference with those rights. The evidence was that dredging and filling would smother and kill the corals and that the structures would endanger small boats.
The rule matters to anyone planning a territory on a reef. On this ruling, which the court said it was limiting to the facts before it, a coastal country does not need to own the seabed or claim the water above it. Its exclusive right to the resources is enough to let a court stop the work. Shallow reefs near a coast are the most tempting sites for building, and they are the very places this rule covers. Nobody ever lived on either project.
grand-capri-atlantis-isle-of-gold.mechanism: United States v. Ray (1970) held that a coastal state can stop building on its continental shelf, the seabed off its coast, without owning that seabed. Its exclusive rights to the resources there are enough for a court to order the work stopped, and US law also required an Army permit for fixed structures on the shelf.

metals-company.story:
The Metals Company is a Canadian-founded business that wants to mine metal-rich nodules from the Pacific floor. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011. The nodules, which contain nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese, lie in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, between Mexico and Hawaii, on seabed that no country owns. Under the Law of the Sea treaty, that seabed is controlled by the International Seabed Authority, and a company needs a contract with the authority and a sponsoring member country.
The company worked within that system by using small Pacific states. Its subsidiary NORI held an exploration contract sponsored by Nauru, and it later bought TOML, sponsored by Tonga. In 2012 DeepGreen agreed to sell 50 percent of its future nickel and copper from the NORI area to the commodity trader Glencore. In 2021 it merged with a listed shell company, a firm with a stock listing and no business, in a $2.9 billion deal, and took its current name.
In June 2021 Nauru told the authority that it intended to begin mining. A rule in the treaty system meant that this started a two-year deadline to finish the mining rules. The deadline passed and the rules were not finished, which left the company with exploration rights and no way to mine.
It then turned to another route. The United States never joined the treaty, and it has its own older law on seabed mining. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the American ocean agency, to speed up permits under that law. Within days the company's American arm applied. NOAA found on 28 April 2026 that the application met the law's information requirements. On 19 August 2026 it opened a 60-day public comment period, which ran to 19 October, with an online public hearing on 13 October. Comments feed into its decision on whether to certify the application, and after that come an environmental impact statement, with more public comment, and a final decision on whether to issue the permit. The law sets no deadline for NOAA to finish. A separate application for an exploration licence over a second area was certified on 26 May 2026, and on 17 August NOAA gave notice that it would prepare an environmental impact statement for it. No licence or permit had been issued as of a securities filing of 24 September 2026, which said there was no assurance that one would be, and which gave the company's expectation that the process would conclude before the end of March 2027. Whether NOAA has certified the main application since comments closed is not known. In its second-quarter 2026 report the company said NOAA's review had slipped by a few months and that it still expected the permit before commissioning its offshore collection system, targeted for the end of 2027.
The authority responded by opening an inquiry into whether NORI and TOML had broken their contracts. The two companies took it to a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal in June 2026, and on 18 July the chamber ordered the authority to respect fair procedure, without suspending the inquiry. The main case is undecided. NORI's contract was extended to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending.
The company stands on both sides of the question. Its subsidiaries hold contracts under the treaty, and its American arm seeks a permit that would bypass that treaty. The United States told the authority in July 2026, by the company's account, that it is not bound by the treaty's seabed mining rules. What remains open is whether one country's permit can give a company a right to mine an area that most of the world has agreed to manage together. The answer will affect anyone hoping to operate outside the shared system with one government's approval.

set.challenge: The companies are suing the Seabed Authority over its inquiry, and the tribunal ordered fair procedure on 18 July 2026 with the main case pending; no American licence or permit had been issued as of 24 September 2026

add_sources.t: Metals Royalty Co Form F-1, filed 24 Sep 2026, SEC

xlii-seastead-phuket.story:
A seastead is a permanent home at sea, and its backers hope to live beyond any country's laws. XLII was a small one, a six-metre-wide cabin raised on a weighted column, paid for and built by a company called Ocean Builders. It was anchored in the Andaman Sea about 14 nautical miles off Phuket, Thailand. Chad Elwartowski, a 46-year-old American bitcoin trader, and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019.
The location was chosen with the law of the sea in mind. A country's full territorial sea ends 12 nautical miles from its coast. From 12 to 24 miles is the contiguous zone, where it has only limited powers such as customs enforcement. Out to 200 miles is the exclusive economic zone, where it controls fish and minerals. Ocean Builders and its supporters relied on the limits these rules place on a coastal state past 12 miles. Elwartowski said 20 more homes would be sold to form a community.
Thailand disagreed. The Thai navy said that the couple had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court and invited others to join, and it treated this as an attack on the country's sovereignty, its right to rule its own territory. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April 2019. Thailand revoked Elwartowski's visa and charged the two under a law carrying life in prison or death. On 22 April navy boats began towing the cabin to shore as evidence.
Ocean Builders said that the cabin sat in the contiguous zone and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its 200-mile economic zone. A senior official urged the couple to come back and fight the charge in court. The charge was under Section 119 of the Criminal Code, on threats to national security. In June 2019 officials said there had been no progress in arresting them, after tracing them to Tarutao island in April. Police had twice asked the couple to present themselves to be formally told of the charge, and they had not done so. On 17 June Elwartowski said on Facebook that the two had married. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged, among them seven Thais and a German. How the case ended in Thailand is not known, and no arrest of the couple is known. Ocean Builders later built floating homes at a marina in Panama, under Panamanian law.
The treaty does limit what a state may do past 12 miles, but a state that sees a threat can act first and argue later, and those living on the platform carried the risk. Their case also shows the problem of ties to land, since Thepdet was a Thai citizen and Elwartowski held a Thai visa, and that gave Thailand direct power over them whatever the status of the water.

add_sources.t: Quién diseñó las casas flotantes en Colón, Panamá América, 27 Sep 2022

tongasat.story:
Geostationary orbit is the ring above the equator where a satellite stays over one spot. Space cannot be owned, but positions there must be shared out so that signals do not interfere. The International Telecommunication Union (ITU), a United Nations agency, keeps the register. Only countries can apply, and a position then belongs in practice to that country to use or license. Tonga is a small kingdom in the South Pacific, and Tongasat is the company that turned this rule into a business. It has been described as a flag of convenience for space, the way a ship might register in a small country.
In 1987 Matt Nilson, a businessman who had moved to Tonga from San Diego to retire, persuaded the king, through Princess Pilolevu, that even a tiny country could apply. The government authorised the venture in April 1988, and in March 1990 Nilson applied for 16 of the 180 slots then available. Intelsat, a satellite operator, and the United States objected. The ITU agreed in March 1991 after he cut the request to six, and Tonga eventually held nine, which made it the sixth-largest claimant of orbital slots. The plan was to rent each slot for $2 million a year, with half the profit going to the government. In practice it charged around $700,000 per transponder, a transponder being one of the radio relays on a satellite.
A company called Rimsat rented slots in 1992, and Nilson was fired in February 1994 after an audit found that he owned Rimsat shares. In 2002 Tongasat acquired Esiafi 1, a satellite already in orbit that had been launched in 1981 as Comstar 4d. China later wanted the slot at 130 degrees East, and Tonga gave way in exchange for grant aid. China paid about US$49.9 million in two parts, in 2008 and 2011, and about 93 percent of it, over US$46 million, went to Tongasat. A public service association and the politician 'Akilisi Pohiva challenged this in court. On 17 August 2018 Lord Chief Justice Paulsen ruled that the company had not been entitled to the money, that it was public money, and that paying it out had broken the law on public funds. He dismissed their claim for repayment, because they had no standing, meaning no legal right, to bring it, and he said the payments could be recovered if the government itself claimed them.
Tongasat appealed. Security for costs is money an appellant must deposit in case it loses and owes the other side's legal fees. Tongasat paid 15,000 pa'anga in March 2019, and in April the appeal court refused its request to bring new evidence. On 31 July it was ordered to pay a further 35,000 pa'anga, about US$15,000, by 1 November, or the appeal would be put on hold. Whether it paid, how the appeal ended and whether any money was returned are not known.
Tongasat shows the legal way a tiny place can earn from space. A rule that treats every recognised state alike gave Tonga standing that no private company could get. It also shows that the right still belongs to the state. A private group with no country behind it could file nothing, and the Tonga case shows the risks that arise when a state hands that right to a private agent, including conflicts of interest and fights over whose money it is.

set.cost: Slots planned at $2 million a year each, with about $700,000 per transponder charged in practice; over US$46 million in Chinese grant aid went to the company
set.challenge: Lost in Tonga's Supreme Court over more than US$46 million in public money; the outcome of its appeal is not known

add_sources.t: Tongasat must pay further $35,000 security, Matangi Tonga, 6 Aug 2019
Tongasat ordered to pay security for costs, Matangi Tonga, 4 Mar 2019

kingdom-of-enenkio.story:
Wake Island is a remote Pacific atoll, a ring of coral, with no native population. The United States has controlled it since 1899. The Marshall Islands, a Pacific nation to the south, also claims it, calling it Ānen Kio. In 1973 Marshallese lawmakers declared that it had always belonged to their people, a claim resting on oral legends and songs.
The Kingdom of EnenKio grew out of that dispute without being part of it. In 1994 Robert F. Moore, a Honolulu resident who said he acted for a Marshallese chief, Murjel Hermios, announced that an independent kingdom existed on Wake and four other atolls, which he said the United States had seized from their rightful native owners. He called himself Minister Plenipotentiary, a title for a senior envoy, and the kingdom issued passports. In 1997 the Marshall Islands Journal reported that it had declared war on the United States and was asking for Marshallese support.
The people it claimed to speak for rejected it. On 23 April 1998 the Marshall Islands government issued a formal note condemning its claims, saying that its representatives were not citizens and had no right to speak for Marshallese landowners.
Moore then turned to investors. He marketed $1 billion in Enenkio Gold War Bonds online, saying they were backed by gold and promising 10 percent compound interest after five years. This brought him under US investment law, which requires bonds offered to the public to be registered and forbids false statements about them. The Securities and Exchange Commission, the American regulator of investments, said no gold or other backing existed and that the bonds had not been registered. On 5 October 2000 it won a temporary order from Judge Susan Mollway in Honolulu that froze his assets and required him to account for the money. He kept offering the bonds on his website and gave no sworn accounting, so the commission asked for him to be held in contempt, meaning punished for disobeying a court. On 23 October he consented, without admitting or denying the allegations, to a permanent ban on breaking those investment laws and to a finding of civil contempt. The judge ordered him to take the offering down within 48 hours and to give the accounting, with a fine of $1,000 for each day he did not. She left for later the question of whether he must give up any money or pay penalties, and what was decided on that is not known.
No state recognises the kingdom. It shows that a seller's claim to be a foreign government does not protect him from the regulator of the place where he actually sits.

set.challenge: A federal judge froze its founder's assets in October 2000, and he then consented to a permanent injunction and a contempt finding

puertopia-sol.story:
Puertopia, later renamed Sol, was a plan by wealthy cryptocurrency investors to build a new city in Puerto Rico, a US territory, in which the money would be virtual and contracts public. They arrived after Hurricane Maria hit in September 2017, as cryptocurrency prices were soaring. Their leader was Brock Pierce, director of the Bitcoin Foundation and co-founder of the blockchain firm Block.One.
The attraction was tax. Under section 933 of the US tax code, an American who genuinely lives in Puerto Rico leaves income from Puerto Rican sources out of federal income tax, while income from elsewhere can still have to be reported to the United States. To count as a resident, the person must pass tests of physical presence, tax home and closer connection to the island. Separately, a Puerto Rican law, Act 22 at that time and now part of Act 60, offered new residents full or partial exemption from Puerto Rico's own income tax on certain capital gains, dividends and interest. Gains that built up before the move are generally not covered. New applications from 2027 may face a 4 percent Puerto Rican rate, and the IRS has been auditing people who claim these benefits since a campaign it began in 2021. One member said they chose the island because the storm had swept everything away, leaving a case for rebuilding, and another investor called it a godsend in the long term.
In early 2018 they rented a 20,000-square-foot hotel in the capital, called the Monastery, as their base, and toured properties where they could have their own airports and docks. They debated buying the Roosevelt Roads Naval Station, 9,000 acres with two deep-water ports. Another resident said they had told him they would buy 250,000 acres and incorporate their own city. Some members thought moving into Old San Juan was enough. For the time being the governor was willing to speak at their conference, and they said they were close to permission for a cryptocurrency bank.
Their idea of a city was limited by law from the start, because the island remains under United States law. A local critic spoke of crypto colonialism, and another Puerto Rican called the island a tax playground for the rich. They are not known to have bought the base or founded a city.

add_sources.t: Act 60 tax compliance and IRS scrutiny, Holland & Knight, 29 Jun 2026

mars-one.story:
Mars One was a small Dutch venture that planned a permanent human colony on Mars with volunteers on a one-way trip, paid for partly by a reality television show. Its chief executive Bas Lansdorp announced it in 2012.
It had two parts, a nonprofit foundation and a for-profit company, Mars One Ventures, registered in Switzerland, with very few staff. It was not an aerospace firm and meant to buy rockets, spacecraft, habitats and suits from outside suppliers, at an estimated $6 billion for the first mission. Early plans sent robots first in 2020 and settlers a few years later, and by 2019 the target had slipped to 2031.
The company said 202,586 people from about 140 countries applied in 2013. Joseph Roche, a physicist among the finalists, said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. Roche and others called it a scam, which it denied, and academics called the plan a suicide mission. Contracts for early design studies with Lockheed Martin and Surrey Satellite Technology ran out.
On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel in Switzerland declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt, with debts of about 1 million euros, and in February an appeals court in the canton of Basel-Stadt upheld the bankruptcy. Lansdorp said the foundation was untouched, but the bankrupt company was the part meant to raise money. No hardware was built.
The law on Mars was never reached. Had a launch gone ahead, the registering country would have kept legal authority over the craft and its crew under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, and a state would have had to authorise the one-way mission. The project ended instead in a Swiss court, over debts of about 1 million euros, far below the $6 billion estimated for the mission.

herzl-palestine-offer.story:
Theodor Herzl, one of the founders of Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, tried in 1896 and 1901 to get Palestine from the Ottoman Empire, which ruled it. The empire was deeply in debt to European powers, whose representatives controlled much of its revenue through a body called the Ottoman Public Debt Administration. The case is on the map as an attempt to buy territory directly from a government, using that debt as the lever.
According to an account published by the Turkish public broadcaster TRT World, he offered £20 million in 1896 for a charter allowing Jews to settle there, a sum that account says would have covered about a fifth of the debt. A charter is a formal grant of rights from a ruler. He worked through intermediaries named Philip de Newlinski and Arminius Vambery, who doubted that Jerusalem could be sold whatever the state of Ottoman finances.
Sultan Abdul Hamid II refused, telling Newlinski that he could not sell even a foot of land because it belonged to his people, who had won the empire with their blood. As ruler and caliph he also drew authority from holding Islam's holy places. Herzl met the sultan in person in 1901 with a different proposal, a company of Jewish financiers in Istanbul that would buy up Ottoman debt over time, in return for autonomy for some land in Palestine as a destination for Jewish migrants. Autonomy means limited self-rule inside a larger state, which is less than the charter he had first sought.
The sultan was interested in consolidating the debt but treated it as a separate matter from settlement, so nothing came of the land proposal.

set.cost: £20 million offered in 1896, according to TRT World

rudd-concession.story:
The Rudd Concession was an 1888 agreement in which King Lobengula of Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, signed away the mineral rights of his kingdom to three men, Charles Rudd, Francis Thompson and Rochfort Maguire, who were agents of the businessman and politician Cecil Rhodes. Rhodes wanted to bring the region into the British Empire, and he needed the concession to win a charter for a company that could annex and govern it. It is on the map as the case of a narrow mining paper turning into a whole country.
Concession seekers kept pressing him, and he feared the Boers of the Transvaal, who wanted land. He held 600 to 800 guns with almost no ammunition. Rudd's party said it wanted only to mine and trade. He reasoned that he would keep his land and gain British protection, and that one powerful holder would end the stream of small prospectors. Younger councillors, the izinDuna, mostly opposed any concession, while older ones were open to it.
The text promised the king £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 cartridges, and either a steamboat with guns on the Zambezi River or £500. In return the three men received complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals in his lands, and the power to do whatever they judged necessary to get them. The king also authorised them to keep out everyone else seeking land or mining rights, and agreed to grant no more concessions without their consent.
According to the missionary Helm, who interpreted, Rudd promised orally that no more than 10 white men would work in the country, that they would not dig near towns and that they would obey the king's laws. None of that was in the written document, so none of it could be enforced. Helm certified that the terms had been explained to the king and his council. Rhodes called the result so gigantic that it was like giving a man the whole of Australia. The version first published left out the rifles, to avoid alarm among the Boers.
From 1889 Lobengula tried to disown the deal, saying that limits agreed orally had been left out, and sent envoys to Queen Victoria, without success. Britain granted a royal charter to Rhodes's British South Africa Company in October 1889, and the company occupied the neighbouring region of Mashonaland in 1890. The charter gave the company what the paper had never given, the power to govern. Its troops conquered Matabeleland in 1893 and 1894, and Lobengula died in exile soon afterwards. The company's charter ended in 1923, when Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing colony.

duran-sun.story:
María Ángeles Durán, a woman from Vigo in Galicia, Spain, claims to own the Sun. Her case raises, in a simple form, the question of who the treaties on outer space bind.
The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says countries cannot claim a planet, a star or any other body in space as national territory. In 2010 Durán went to a notary and had her statement recorded that she owned the Sun. Her argument is that the treaty speaks of states and does not bind individuals. A notary's job is to confirm that a person appeared and made a statement, and it does not test whether the statement is true. She threatened to charge people for using solar power, and she sold plots on the Sun on the auction site eBay at one euro per square metre.
About two years after she opened her account, eBay removed the listings under its policy on intangible goods and blocked her account. According to Durán, eBay said the Sun "is not tangible and can't be sold", and she insisted it was a real product. She sued in court number 5 of Alcobendas, near Madrid, seeking 10,000 euros. The court admitted the claim, and at a conciliation hearing in July 2015, a meeting meant to settle a case without trial, the two sides did not agree, so the case was to go to trial.
Reports differ on what the courts did next. A report from June 2015 said a Spanish court recognised her claim and let her pursue the dispute, with a first hearing set for 17 June 2015. The Mexican newspaper Excelsior said in 2022 that the court declared itself competent and gave her standing to sue, and it dated recognition of her ownership to 2012, without citing documents. The Spanish site Genbeta later wrote that the court dismissed her case and that a Spanish court said in 2016 that a person cannot legally own the Sun, but it names no court document and credits Excelsior, whose article does not say this. The Spanish site Xataka repeats the dismissal, also crediting Excelsior. How the case ended is not known.
Letting someone sue is a different thing from finding that she owns the Sun. A court can hear a dispute between a seller and a website without deciding whether the goods exist as property. No confirmed court ruling says she owns it. No one is known to have paid her for sunlight. Durán's point is that Article II of the treaty bars national appropriation and names no individuals, and lawyers still argue about it. Article VI answers part of the argument. Countries bear responsibility for what non-governmental bodies do in space, and those bodies need a country's authorisation and continuing supervision. An American case went against a similar claimant. Gregory Nemitz claimed the asteroid Eros and sued NASA after it landed a probe there in 2001. By his own account, a federal court and an appeals court dismissed the claim as a matter of law for lack of a cognizable legal theory, without examining the claim itself. To be real, though, ownership has to be backed by a state's courts and police, and the treaty bars states from claiming the land that would underpin such a title.
